title.official: How to make claim against co-defendant

division.heading: Actions Started by Statement of Claim

operative_text.controlling:
3.43(1)  If a defendant claims a contribution or indemnity, or both,
against a co-defendant under the Tort-feasors Act or the
Contributory Negligence Act,
(a) the defendant may file and serve on a co-defendant a
notice in Form 15 claiming a remedy under either or both
of those Acts,
(b) neither the defendant nor the co-defendant need file a
pleading in respect of a claim or defence under those Acts
unless the Court otherwise orders, and
(c) a third party claim need not be filed and served on the
co-defendant.
(2)  The notice claiming contribution must be filed and served on
the co-defendant within 20 days after the date on which the
defendant files the statement of defence or demand for notice.
(3)  A claim under subrule (1) must be determined at the trial of the
plaintiff’s claim against the defendant, or if there is no trial, as
directed by the Court.

BOOK_A.related_provisions: 3.44 (third party claims) A defendant wishing indemnity or contribution from a co-defendant can issue a third party notice against him or her.But if they are both defendants and the claim over is within theTort- Feasors Actor theContributory Negligence Act, a simple written notice instead will suffice.The notice traditionally does not recite facts.Its effect seems to be much the same as a third party notice. The court would not allow a 5-year time extension to issue a R.3.43 notice. Some cases discuss problems with such claims among defendants where one defendant settles with the plaintiff. A notice under R.3.43 makes those parties"adverse"for discovery purposes. The usual law extends to releases and settlements, so they can bar liability and so bar a claim for contribution among tortfeasors. Does a notice to co-defendant survive discontinuance of the main suit, so a judge used R.1.4 to order the plaintiff not to discontinue without leave. *Subdivision 6 Third Party Claims *WhenThird Party Claim May be Filed*

BOOK_B.title: How to make claim against co-defendant

commentary.text: Rule 3.43 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.43. 1. Purpose of Rule “Rule 77 is a new rule introducing a new procedure for issues between the defendants and provides for the service of a notice making the claim over which will be disposed of at the trial. This is in lieu of third party notice.”“The Alberta Rules of Court—1969” (1969), 7 Alta. Law Rev. 190, J.H. Laycraft, Q.C., and W.A. Stevenson, at 191, as quoted by Master Funduk in Wurtz v. Nobis (1981), 15 Alta. L.R. (2d) 1 at 4 (Master). And in another case Master Funduk stated: Rule 77 is a truncated third party procedure between co-defendants which can be used by a defendant against a co-defendant in limited situations. Meier v. Honda Motor Co. (1991), 113 A.R. 241 at 243 (Master). 2. Scope of Rule Notices to co-defendant are permitted under R. 77. They may be filed in lieu of serving a third party notice, but not, it appears, in all cases … I understand the rule to mean that a notice to co-defendant will be permitted to replace the third party notice only when the claim to indemnity arises from the Tort-Feasors Act, R.S.A. 1980, c. T-6, and the Contributory Negligence Act, R.S.A. 1980, c. C-23. The latter statute speaks of apportioning damages between two or more persons at fault. The former deals with contribution and indemnity as between tortfeasors. Peace Hills Trust Co. v. Professional Property Management Ltd. (1992), 83 Alta. L.R. (2d) 357 (Q.B.) at 359, per MacCallum J.
